cards.title: One-Benefit Email Framework
cards.summary: Build repeatable campaigns around a single product benefit so the takeaway sticks in three seconds.
cards.use_when: Planning your monthly email calendar and needing evergreen campaign angles for each product in the store.
steps: List 10+ distinct benefits per product, one benefit per email.
Spread them out at roughly two per month (five months of coverage).
State only one benefit per send; naming six benefits makes customers remember none.
Lead with the benefit in the headline and keep the email visually simple, as in the 'banish festive fogginess' and Seed '61% of people experience digestive discomfort' examples.
Reuse these campaigns repeatedly; repetition is how customers remember.
caveats: The 'three-second read' and two-per-month cadence are the source's heuristics, not tested benchmarks.

cards.title: One-Feature Email: Selling Ingredient and Spec Differentiation
cards.summary: Feature a single ingredient, material or spec to distinguish a product that otherwise sounds identical to competitors.
cards.use_when: Writing product emails when every competitor claims the same benefit (e.g. protein powder that all says 'gain muscle').
steps: Write out every material or ingredient in the product; each can anchor its own email.
Pick one feature per email rather than a benefits-only pitch — features like 'pre-digestive enzyme' or an AI capability are things people actively want to know.
Assume the customer does not know what you consider common sense (David Ogilvy's point); spell the feature out.
Show examples like 'tamanu oil' or 'what we mean by instantised creatine' — one specific item per email, not a list of five.
For non-consumables, substitute the material or construction detail (e.g. clothing fabric composition).
caveats: The source pushes back on 'benefits not features' as an oversimplification; both angles have a place.

cards.title: Single-FAQ Email to Kill Objections
cards.summary: Answer one frequently asked customer question per email to overcome objections and quietly position the product.
cards.use_when: Mining support tickets and reviews for purchase objections to turn into campaign content.
steps: Gather real questions from your support team and product reviews.
Pick ONE question per email; a long FAQ dump gets ignored.

Answer directly, then bridge into why your product solves it — e.g. 'how long until creatine works' answered with a timeframe and a shop link, or 'does whitening hurt teeth' answered with the damage-free alternative.
Think like an alien who just discovered your product: what would they ask?
Note that what's obvious to you as the industry expert is not obvious to the buyer.
caveats: Timeframe numbers in examples are brand-specific; use your own verified claims.

cards.title: 'What's Inside' Email for Bundles and Consumables
cards.summary: Unpack everything included with an order in a skimmable list to remove pre-purchase uncertainty.
cards.use_when: Selling bundles, kits or consumable products where buyers don't know exactly what they'll receive.
steps: List every component of the bundle or product in a skimmable list format.
Include free extras customers don't know about (installation guides, video guides, replacement parts) — brands often give these away without ever telling buyers.
For consumables, list out everything in the food, beverage or supplement so buyers know what's entering their body.
Use examples like an AG1-style unboxing of the welcome kit, or a 'seven super ingredients' list that keeps each item brief.
Spread this across multiple emails rather than cramming everything into one.
caveats: Keep each item short; the goal is scannability, not depth.

cards.title: How-It's-Made and How-To-Use Emails
cards.summary: Turn your production process or usage instructions into a story-driven email that signals quality and removes complexity objections.
cards.use_when: Reducing hesitation on a product that seems complicated, or building brand story for a physical product.
steps: For 'how it's made': list every step from material gathering through factory, warehouse and shipment, or spotlight a single stage (e.g. 'we run every ingredient through three filters').
Present the process with clear graphics or a simple A-to-Z sequence — a beer-style 'malt, mash, boil, ferment, bottle, age' layout works well.
For 'how to use': write step-by-step instructions by actually using the product yourself and recording what you do.
If the product is simple to use, reframe as 'how to get the most out of X' or 'how to style X' instead.
Push the usage content into your post-purchase flow too; it fits both pre- and post-buy.
caveats: Don't assume the customer knows your process even if all your competitors do the same thing — saying it still signals quality.

cards.title: Back-in-Stock Email Leveraging Popularity and Urgency
cards.summary: Use the back-in-stock angle to combine popularity proof with scarcity, even for products that never truly sold out.
cards.use_when: New inventory arrives, or you want a high-urgency campaign angle on restocked or returned items.
steps: Track when products or collections come back into stock.
Draft a full feature email around the return — e.g. 'the Spidey Suds is back', 'the full glass is back in a new style'.
Frame with limited-time language ('only here for a limited time') to add urgency.
If a product didn't actually go out of stock, you can still use the restock angle when you receive new inventory.
Buying signals to lean on: something went out of stock, so it's popular, and it may go out again.
caveats: This is an attention angle, not a factual emergency; don't fabricate sell-outs you didn't have.

cards.title: Trending Product Email — Frame Future, Not Past
cards.summary: Promote best-performing products by framing them as upcoming trends rather than last season's favorites.
cards.use_when: Highlighting top sellers or building seasonal collection emails on your store.
steps: Pick the product or collection performing well and feature it.
Frame as future trending ('these have been heating up; hottest trend for summer 2024') rather than past trending ('what was popular last summer').
Create curated product selections linking to a collection page in Shopify-type platforms to lift conversions on the click-through.
Lean into seasons whenever possible — seasonal selling performs especially well.
Send these frequently; the source says you can't send too many.
caveats: 'Future beats past trending' is the source's observed pattern, not a proven conversion benchmark.

cards.title: Reviews and Testimonials Email for Social Proof
cards.summary: Feature a small number of customer reviews or social comments to prove legitimacy and trigger herd behavior.
cards.use_when: Building trust for a newer brand or nudging hesitant subscribers with peer proof.
steps: Pull real reviews from your product pages and site.
Use a maximum of two long reviews, or a handful of short ones — as in the Greens example using dated social-media comments.
Include social media comments where possible; recent dated comments boost credibility.
Keep the email short and simple, essentially just quotes plus a CTA.
Testimonials do two jobs: prove you're a legit brand that delivers, and show others already bought and are happy.
caveats: Only use real testimonials; the source emphasizes authenticity.

cards.title: Us vs Them Comparison Email
cards.summary: Compare your product against competitors in a clear table to help buyers choose you without begging for the sale.
cards.use_when: Competitive categories where buyers are weighing alternatives before purchase.
steps: Build a simple comparison table with digestible points — 'why we shine' or 'this product vs that product'.
Show facts; do not beg for the purchase or lose frame, which increases sales resistance.
Keep it skimmable so the customer can instantly see the differentiators.
End with a clear CTA like 'shop now' and product link.
Angle can also be used for product-vs-product within your own line.
caveats: Keep claims accurate and verifiable; a table format doesn't excuse unsubstantiated comparisons.

cards.title: Myth vs Fact Email
cards.summary: Bust common industry misconceptions to overcome objections with an engaging, curiosity-driven premise.
cards.use_when: Your niche has persistent misinformation (sunscreen, supplements, etc.) that blocks purchases.
steps: Identify common misconceptions buyers hold about your product category.
Structure emails as 'myth: X / fact: Y', either one myth per email or rapid-fire several.
Use an intriguing headline, as in the sunscreen myth-busting example with multiple 'myth busted' sections.
Keep copy punchy — customers won't read long explanations.
Consider a series of myth emails; the source says series have worked well historically.
caveats: Long myth-vs-fact copy underperforms; condense and make it scannable.

cards.title: Blog Promo Email That Sells the Click
cards.summary: Use a sneak peek to drive traffic to a blog post, warming subscribers and enabling soft-sell product placement.
cards.use_when: You have blog content and want engagement that moves people down the funnel without a hard pitch.
steps: Use an existing blog post with an intriguing headline.
Give only a sneak peek — withhold enough that clicking is worthwhile; do not dump the whole article into the email.
Sell the click aggressively via prominent buttons and a 'read more' / 'get the scoop' CTA.
Place product recommendations further down in the email after the article context.
Rationale: a subscriber clicking a blog is already committing to browsing, making later site shopping more likely; blog emails read as soft-sell and still drive sales.
caveats: The source criticizes its own examples for giving too much info; reduce to preserve click incentive.

cards.title: Research Study Highlight Email
cards.summary: Cite a published study related to your niche to position the brand as an industry leader and lateral proof.
cards.use_when: Looking for high-credibility campaign content that your list rarely sees.
steps: Search Google Scholar for your industry niche; also possible via ChatGPT with a prompt.
Spend no more than a few minutes; read the abstract to judge applicability.
Pick a study that either busts a myth or supports an ingredient/material you use.
Connect it to your brand even if it's not a study of your own product — e.g. 'new study reveals the link between soft gums and inflammation', then show your product solves soft gums.
Lay out the study with a clear breakdown and a learn-more CTA.
caveats: The source says this shouldn't take more than a couple minutes to find a decent one.

cards.title: Holiday Email Using Obscure Holidays
cards.summary: Anchor fun emails to unusual daily holidays connected to your niche rather than only major holidays.
cards.use_when: Filling campaign calendar gaps and adding engagement without overt promotion.
steps: Find random holidays; use sites like checkiday.com, blank calendar pages, or ChatGPT.
Pick one that connects to a product or niche (e.g. National Irish Coffee Day used by Jameson, National Hiking Day used by AllTrails).
Build a light, fun email around it with a natural product tie-in.
You can still send standard major-holiday emails; these add incremental volume and engagement.
caveats: Keep the tie-in plausible; a forced holiday-to-product link can feel gimmicky.

cards.title: 15 Rapid-Fire Campaign Angenres for Ecommerce Lists
cards.summary: A catalog of niche-agnostic email angles you can bolt onto a calendar when ideas run dry.
cards.use_when: When building monthly calendars and needing more micro-topic campaign angles across the store.
steps: Progress update: share company milestones and achievements — people like being part of a growing brand.
Customer transformation and before/after: real before-and-after narratives of product impact.
Puzzles and riddles: brain teasers related to your industry as a fun break.
Note from the founder: personal CEO message with news or insights.
Gift guide: curated recommendations (e.g. wedding season, summer).
Treat yourself: self-care excuse to buy.
Media publication: coverage in news or Shark Tank and similar.
Behind the scenes: warehouse/office footage or product stories.
Tips and tricks: valuable quick advice.
UGC: tagged customer photos, reviews and influencer content.
Sneak peeks: reward subscribers with early looks.
Flashback/Throwback: nostalgic content and past milestones.
Staff picks: bestsellers framed as individual staff favorites.
Brand values: showcase what the brand stands for.
caveats: Not one campaign type; use selectively against your list's appetite.

cards.title: Building a Monthly Campaign Calendar
cards.summary: Sequence anchor dates, supplementary sends and micro-topic campaigns into a structured monthly calendar.
cards.use_when: Turning a library of campaign ideas into an actual send schedule for your store.
steps: Step 1: Determine important dates — holidays, product launches, sale dates — and insert them into the calendar first so everything else builds around them.
Step 2: Add supplementary emails around those anchors — reminders for sales, teasers for launches.
Step 3: Fill remaining gaps with micro-topic campaigns (one-benefit, one-feature, FAQ, etc.).
Aim for three to four campaigns per week, each on a micro-topic.
Example structure: a St Patrick's Day 20%-off sale, a new product drop, supplementary emails around each, and micro-topics filling the rest.
caveats: The three-to-four-per-week cadence is the source's heuristic from agency work; adjust to list health.

cards.title: Segmentation: Dynamic Segments vs Static Lists
cards.summary: Understand segments as dynamic, self-updating subsets so you can send the right content to the right slice.
cards.use_when: Designing list architecture in Klaviyo or similar before building campaigns and flows.
steps: Distinguish lists (static, flat collections of people) from segments (dynamic, updating in real time based on criteria).
In Klaviyo, lists and segments live under the same area but segments are the dynamic ones.
Start with basics: email open behavior, click behavior, frequency.
Intermediate: recent store activity like abandoned cart, recent purchase.
Advanced: flow-specific engagement or product-category interest.
Before hypersegmenting (e.g. by favorite color), weigh the tradeoff — the source argues three to four broad campaigns to 50,000 will beat one to two narrow campaigns to 10,000 '99 times out of 100'.
caveats: That ratio is the source's claimed experience, not a measured guarantee; they do say there's a time and place for segmentation.

cards.title: Email Engagement Segments for Deliverability
cards.summary: Build the core engaged/unengaged suppression sets that protect inbox placement and control sending costs.
cards.use_when: Setting up your base sending architecture so campaigns never blast the full list.
steps: Create an X-day engaged segment — 'opened an email at least once in last 60 days OR clicked in last 60 days' (the OR guards against missed open tracking).
Add 'has not bounced an email ever' to exclude dead/fake addresses.
Decide the X window: start at 30 days if new to segmentation, then expand to 60, 90, 120 as open rates climb.
Target at least 40% opens before expanding; when opens hit ~50%, open the window to the next tier and repeat.
Create an unengaged members segment (subscribed, opened at least once historically, but no open/click in ~90 days) and email them around once per month — or suppress entirely.
Never send general campaigns to the whole list except major moments like Black Friday, because non-openers damage deliverability with inbox providers.
caveats: The step-ladder and 40-50% thresholds are the source's recommendations, not universal benchmarks.

cards.title: Store-Engagement Segments to Find Funnel Leaks
cards.summary: Segment by on-site behavior to spot where buyers drop off and target them directly.
cards.use_when: Diagnosing conversion loss and building targeted campaigns beyond flows.
steps: Viewed a product at least once in past 30 days but no purchase = interested customers.
Added to cart or started checkout in past 30 days but no purchase = high likelihood to purchase; engage these hard.
Placed an order = recent buyers.
Placed five-plus orders = VIP customers.
Viewed at least three products without purchasing = window shoppers.
Use these to track where people are lost — e.g. lots of product views but few add-to-carts signals a product-page problem.
Targeted campaigns (new colorway, special discount) can be sent only to product-category-interested segments without bothering the rest of the list.
caveats: Mostly used alongside flows; campaigns are added on top, not instead.

cards.title: High Potential Purchaser Segment
cards.summary: Create a segment of recent site-active non-buyers to send extra nudges on top of the engaged list.
cards.use_when: Running an extra sale or push to people who are actively shopping but haven't purchased.
steps: Definition: subscribed AND placed zero orders in past 30 days AND (active on site OR viewed product OR added to cart OR started checkout in past 30 days).
Use OR conditions between the activity triggers as a safety net for missed event tracking.
Send these people one to two extra emails per month on top of your engaged list sends — a targeted sale or extra push.
Reserve certain offers for this segment rather than the whole list so you don't discount for everyone.
caveats: Some conditions overlap intentionally; the source keeps them to guard against broken triggers.

cards.title: VIP Segment Built on Purchase Count
cards.summary: Define VIPs by order count rather than spend to make milestones predictable and promotable.
cards.use_when: Designing a loyalty/VIP segment and corresponding email cadence.
steps: Base definition: subscribed AND placed an order at least five times all-time.
Prefer purchase count over total spend because spend thresholds are harder to predict — someone at $900 toward $1,000 might buy a $20 item and miss the goal, causing frustration.
With a count-based threshold, after the fourth purchase you can notify them they're one order from VIP and a free gift.
Send VIPs at most one extra email per month on top of the engaged list.
Run a welcome flow for anyone entering the segment — thank them and give exclusive content or a generous offer.
Send a VIP-only offer at least once a quarter.
caveats: Five orders is the source's illustrative threshold; use one that fits your purchase frequency.

cards.title: Winback and Unengaged: Distinguishing Two Recovery Segments
cards.summary: Keep email-unengaged and past-customer winback segments separate because they solve different problems.
cards.use_when: Building reactivation and repurchase campaigns for your list.
steps: Unengaged members = email-side: subscribed and once engaged but no open/click in ~90 days; email roughly monthly with a comeback offer.
Winback potential customers = purchase-side: past buyers who haven't purchased in a while; also email ~one extra per month on top of engaged sends.
Set the winback window to the store's typical inter-purchase interval — hot tubs might be years, supplements much shorter.
Regular campaigns to the engaged list can also be sent to the unengaged once a month as a low-effort recovery attempt.
Don't send every campaign to unengaged people; it drags down open rates and sender reputation.
caveats: The 90-day threshold isn't sacred; 120 days is similarly acceptable per the source.

cards.title: Predictive Analytics for AOV, CLV and Replenishment Timing
cards.summary: Use Klaviyo predictive analytics to target high spenders, VIPs and near-repurchase groups.
cards.use_when: Upgrading segmentation beyond basic behavior to optimize offers and timing.
steps: Open Klaviyo predictive analytics and inspect average order value cohorts.
If store AOV is ~$50, build a segment with AOV $100+ and target them with bundle deals or large inventory-clearing offers.
Segment by predicted customer lifetime value to identify VIPs.
Segment by average time between purchases — e.g. if a cohort reorders every 45 days, fire a reminder flow around day 40.
Segment by predicted gender to tailor product recommendations and creative.
caveats: The source notes Klaviyo predictions aren't perfect — treat as directional data.

cards.title: Location Segmentation for Pop-Ups and Regional Offers
cards.summary: Segment by geography to target local events, region-specific stores and compliance needs.
cards.use_when: Running pop-up shops, in-person events or country-specific storefronts.
steps: Build segments by city, state or country.
For an in-person event, target subscribers in that city (e.g. a San Diego pop-up).
Use location to handle compliance requirements and localized store experiences across countries.
Also useful for brand-headquarters-area promotions.
caveats: Requires reliable location data; some subscribers won't have it.

cards.title: Cadence and Content Rule: Send Three to Four Emails a Week
cards.summary: High-frequency, high-quality campaigning to engaged segments outperforms low-frequency sending.
cards.use_when: Deciding how many campaigns per week to run and worried about unsubscribes.
steps: Send three to four campaigns per week to the engaged segment, per the source's experience across 50+ ecommerce brands.
Keep content strong; the source observed lower unsubscribe rates at this frequency than sending once a week.
Each campaign should be built on a distinct micro-topic so the list doesn't fatigue.
Frequency only works when paired with engagement segmentation; sending that much to unengaged people backfires on deliverability.
Use the calendar structure: metrics (3-4/wk) and topic diversity are both required.
caveats: The source's observation, not a universal rule; test against your own unsubscribe and spam rates.
